summary: A stepwise method with the compensation formulas and two oxygenation tools.

items: 2. PaCO₂ — high = respiratory acidosis component; low = respiratory alkalosis component
5. Expected compensation — Winter's formula for a metabolic acidosis: expected PaCO₂ = (1.5 × HCO₃⁻) + 8 ± 2. Actual PaCO₂ outside this range → a mixed disorder.
6. If a metabolic acidosis is present, calculate the anion gap (see the calculator).
7. If the AG is elevated, calculate the delta-delta to look for a concurrent non-gap process.

body.text: A-a gradient = P(A)O₂ − P(a)O₂, where on room air at sea level P(A)O₂ ≈ 150 − (1.25 × PaCO₂). Normal upper limit ≈ (Age / 4) + 4 mmHg. A wider gradient points to a diffusion / V-Q mismatch / shunt problem rather than pure hypoventilation.

The curve is sigmoidal, not linear. At SpO₂ 88% (a ~10-point drop from normal) the PaO₂ is only ~50 mmHg — tissues are getting roughly half the oxygen they would at a normal saturation. A small SpO₂ drop in the high-80s is a much bigger fall in delivered O₂ than the same drop in the mid-90s. If oxygenation is genuinely in question, get an ABG PaO₂ rather than trusting the saturation number.

P50 = the PaO₂ at which haemoglobin is 50% saturated — the single-number summary of where the whole curve sits. Normal adult P50 ≈ 26.6 mmHg (37 °C, pH 7.4). Lower P50 = left shift, higher O₂ affinity (fetal Hb ≈ 18–19; also alkalosis, hypothermia, low 2,3-DPG, carboxyhaemoglobin, methaemoglobin) — holds O₂ tighter, unloads less at the tissue. Higher P50 = right shift, lower affinity (acidosis, hypercapnia, fever, high 2,3-DPG) — favours tissue unloading.
